notes.meaning: "Therefore" looks back to chapter 2, where Jesus is shown as our caring helper. The readers are "holy brothers": one family, set apart for God. Their calling comes from heaven and leads to heaven. They are told to fix their minds on Jesus. As "apostle" (one sent by God) He brings God's message to us. As "high priest" He pleads our cause before God. He holds both jobs at once, the jobs that Moses and Aaron held separately.

Jesus was faithful to the Father who gave Him His work, and He carried it out fully. The writer honors Moses too. God Himself called Moses faithful in all His house (Numbers 12:7). Here "house" means God's family, the people of Israel. The writer first shows how the two are alike, because his Jewish readers thought very highly of Moses.

Jesus deserves more glory than Moses, just as a builder deserves more honor than the house he built. The "house" is God's people, the church. Moses was a member and leader inside that house. Christ is the one who built it. So Christ stands far above Moses.

Every house has a builder, and God is the builder of everything. Christ built God's house, the church, and only God could build it. So the verse shows that Christ is God, and therefore far greater than Moses or any creature.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators read "God" here as the Father, who founded the house. Christ is then the Son set over it. Some admit the reasoning is hard to pin down.

notes.meaning: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house. The word means an honored attendant, not a slave. His laws and worship practices were a witness pointing ahead to the good news that God would later speak through His Son.

Christ is not a servant in the house. He is the Son over it, its rightful owner and ruler. All believers together are His house. But we must hold firmly to our confidence and our joyful hope. Starting well is not enough; we must keep going to the end.

differ.view: Holding fast to the end is the proof that someone truly belongs to Christ's family. Falling away shows they never really did.
We are Christ's house now, and we will stay His house to the end, if we hold fast our faith and hope.

notes.meaning: The writer quotes Psalm 95 as the Holy Spirit speaking, so these words are God's own. "Today" means now, whenever God speaks to us. To "hear His voice" means to listen and obey. We should not put it off until tomorrow.

To harden your heart is to make it stiff and deaf to God's voice. "Rebellion" and "testing" stand for two place names, Meribah and Massah. There Israel complained about having no water and doubted that God was with them (Exodus 17). A hard heart is the root of all other sins.

differ.view: People harden their own hearts by stubborn choice and can blame no one else. Yet by nature everyone has a hard heart, and only God can soften it.
Israel could have been saved but would not. No decree of God kept them out; they chose to sin and not believe.

notes.meaning: Israel tested God by demanding proof and pushing His patience. They did this even while they watched His works: the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock. This went on for forty years, which made their ingratitude even worse.

God was angry and grieved with that generation. Scripture uses human words here to describe how He felt. Their hearts kept wandering away, and they never learned or loved His ways. Sin grieves God, especially sin by His own people, yet He waited a long time before acting.

God's oath shows a firm, settled decision. This happened after the people refused to enter the land when the spies came back (Numbers 14). "My rest" first meant the land of Canaan. Canaan was also a picture of the rest of heaven.

Now the writer turns the story into a warning: watch out! A heart that refuses to trust God is a wicked heart, and it leads to turning away from Him. God is the "living God," real and not like lifeless idols. To walk away from Christ is to walk away from God Himself.

The cure is to encourage one another every day. Even the strongest Christian needs help from others, and we should care about each person. "Today" lasts only while life and God's offer last. Sin is a liar. It looks good but destroys, and each sin makes the heart harder.

Believers share in Christ. They are joined to Him, like a branch to a vine, and receive His life and blessings. This holds true if we keep the confidence we had at the start firm to the very end. We should keep the same spirit we began with.

differ.view: True believers will persevere, kept by God's power. Warnings like this are one of the ways Christ keeps them going.
Holding fast is not a condition for staying saved but the evidence of it. Our union with Christ rests on God's eternal love.
The "if" is real: we keep sharing in Christ only if we hold fast. A believer can fall from grace and be lost.
The readers have something they could lose. Staying faithful to the end is needed to receive what God promised.

notes.meaning: The writer repeats the psalm to show that it speaks to us, not just to people long ago. God keeps speaking to us every day. So for as long as it is "today," while life lasts, we must keep listening and not harden our hearts.

Who rebelled? The very people Moses led out of Egypt, who had seen God's great rescue. Nearly the whole generation turned against God, with only a few exceptions like Joshua and Caleb. Great blessings do not keep anyone safe from falling.

God was angry with those who sinned, and they died in the desert over those forty years (Numbers 14:29). God is never angry without a just reason. This does not mean every one of them was shut out of heaven. Moses and Aaron also died before entering the land.

God swore that those who disobeyed would never enter His rest. Their disobedience came from unbelief: they did not trust the Lord their God (Deuteronomy 1:32). In Hebrews, unbelief and disobedience go hand in hand.

So the lesson is plain: unbelief kept them out. They were unable to enter, even though later they wanted to. Unbelief was the root of all their other sins. We should beware of it and live a life of trusting God.
